headline: FieldOS: A Complete Field Service Platform Built in Just 10 Hours
summary: A developer details how he built a comprehensive field service platform, including the user-facing app and backend systems, in approximately ten hours of real-time work.
details: The final part of the FieldOS series focuses on building the user-facing application that technicians, dispatchers, and customers interact with. This app provides a unified login with role-specific views, ensuring accessibility for everyone involved in the field service process.

Wiring the real interface exposed several bugs that isolation testing missed. These included incorrect sorting of inventory due to quantities being treated as text instead of numbers, and a maintenance schedule date shifting due to timezone differences. These issues were resolved by implementing explicit handling of data types and timezones.

Further issues arose from naming conflicts between the app's internal storage and a specific web page's address, causing errors when accessing the equipment page. Additionally, an automatic invoice-drafting feature from an earlier part was not being reset during demo sessions, leading to a buildup of draft invoices. Both problems were fixed by addressing the naming conflict and ensuring the reset process cleaned up all generated data.

The author emphasizes that the primary goal of building FieldOS was to accurately determine the real cost of such a project. By meticulously tracking all development time, he gained valuable insights into project pricing.

Across all three parts, the core system took roughly three hours, nine add-ons took about two and a half hours, and the final app took just under five hours. This totals approximately ten hours to build a complete, connected field service platform.

This ten-hour development time challenges traditional hourly pricing models. The author argues that pricing should reflect the value and replacement cost of the system for a business, rather than the developer's hourly rate, especially when it replaces years of subscription software fees.

headline: Google Pixel 11: AI features shine despite price hike and RAM cut
summary: The Pixel 11 Pro is Google's most powerful phone yet, but comes with a higher price and less RAM. AI features are a major focus, with Google still leading the competition in this area.
details: Google's new Pixel 11 lineup has arrived, with reviewers noting significant AI integration across the devices. While the Pixel 11 Pro boasts impressive AI capabilities, it also sees a $100 price increase and a reduction in RAM compared to its predecessor.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold, despite its upgrades, retains a chunky design and misses out on some features found in the regular Pixel 11 Pro, such as Pro Res Zoom. Reviewers suggest that without a strong push beyond the existing Pixel ecosystem, it may struggle to attract new users.

Despite the increased cost and reduced RAM, the standard Pixel 11 is still considered the best option for most users, including those switching from iPhone. Its significant upgrades from older Pixel models make it a compelling entry point into the Android ecosystem.

The Pixel Watch 5 is described as a 'fantastic smartwatch... eventually.' While it currently lacks some features, it does enough to justify its price increase, offering a solid user experience that is expected to improve with future updates.

Beyond the Pixel line, HP's Omnibook X is highlighted as an impressive ultraportable Windows laptop, praised for its attention to fundamental features. The Pebble Time 2 is also noted for its appeal to those seeking a less feature-heavy smartwatch experience.

The review roundup also covers other gadgets, including Alienware's 39-inch curved gaming display, Pokémon Champions, the GoPro Mission 1 Pro ILS, Panasonic Lumix L10 cameras, the Nimble SharePower, and Sony's wearable air conditioner.
